Loi 94 : incompréhension et peur face à: Bill 94: Confusion and Fear Over a Law Applied Unevenly
Des éducatrices portant le hijab dénonce: Educators who wear the hijab denounce the inconsistent application of Bill 94 in school centres.
<strong>Adopté le 30 octobre 2025, le pr: Since Bill 94 was passed on October 30, 2025, hundreds of dismissals have been feared in the school system, in the Montréal region alone. Faced with uncertainty over acquired rights, school service centres asked the Ministry of Education for clarification. A memo sent on March 18 by Deputy Minister Carole Arav clarified how the law is to be applied – and made it possible to “bring back” some staff.
<strong>Toutefois, des éducatrices porta: Yet educators who wear the hijab, recalled or sidelined this April, describe an uneven and unpredictable implementation of Bill 94, marked by contradictory decisions – all of it fuelling confusion, fear and a loss of trust in the system.
Dans le hall d’entrée d’un établissement: In the entrance hall of a school on Gouin Street in Pierrefonds, a first group of women talk in low voices while waiting for others to arrive and for the meeting to begin. They don’t all know each other, but all of them are affected by the recent application of Bill 94 in their workplaces.
Certaines ont été appelées à reprendre l: Some have been called back to their positions after being initially removed. Others were given the opposite instruction: take off their hijab or leave their jobs. Between these two situations, there is no apparent consistency. In the scraps of information they exchange, they confirm what each of them already knew: from one school service centre (CSS) to another, and sometimes from one school to another, the very logic behind the decisions differs.
Les témoignages convergent vers un const: The testimonies converge on one conclusion: in practice, the law does not produce a uniform framework, and that leaves room for interpretation. “This ambiguity means that almost every institution and every school service centre has its own interpretation of how to apply the law, which has raised the requirements,” explains Samer Majzoub, president of the Canadian Muslim Forum (CMF), which organized the meeting.
Ce soir, une trentaine de femmes portant: Tonight, about thirty women who wear the Muslim headscarf, all employees of school service centres in Montréal and Laval, are taking part in this CMF initiative, which “aims to support people affected by the changing legislative situation in Quebec by offering them a space to communicate and the chance to obtain personalized legal and social advice.”
Les échanges entre les participantes rév: The conversations among participants reveal the difficulty they all share in grasping the rules that apply to their situation. The criteria evolve, the decisions change, and the answers vary depending on who is asked. Confusion and fear – the faces express the same anxieties. And there is anger too. “There are no clear instructions. The result is that the situation has become vague and random, with everyone acting on their own intentions,” Samer Majzoub continues.
La réunion dure jusque tard dans la nuit: The meeting runs late into the night, with a lawyer present. One educator reports that on several occasions her status was redefined multiple times within a few hours. First deemed not to be covered by the law, she was then asked to provide explanations, before finally being denied the possibility of benefiting from acquired rights. Others describe the opposite: an initial refusal, followed by a call back to work.
Au cœur de ces changements, il y a la no: At the heart of these changes is the notion of “acquired rights,” whose interpretation varies. L.C.*, an educator in Laval, says she was called back after a “new analysis” of her case. “They said: ‘We’ve broadened our understanding of the word “function”’ […] They created categories and sent us tables. They kind of played with words,” she explains.
Les éducatrices « repêchées » sont celle: The educators who were “brought back” are, notably, those who changed positions within the same job category. Those who changed categories, or employers, cannot benefit from what is commonly called the “grandfather clause,” that is, the acquired rights clause.
Les chiffres de cette opération sont par: The figures for this operation are partial for now. At the CSSDM, there are already<l1> 150 educators who have been laid off</l1>. At the Centre de services scolaire de Laval, about forty support staff members (educators, special education technicians, monitors) found themselves on authorized unpaid leave after the measures came into effect. At the same time, the CSSL indicates in an email to our newsroom, about 45 employees who wore a religious symbol agreed to remove it in order to keep their jobs.
Selon la même source, la révision de l’a: According to the same source, the review of how acquired rights are applied, begun in March, allowed 164 employees to return to their positions as of April 13, with 2 others due to do so in the following days. Other files are still under review.
Pour les éducatrices réunies à Pierrefon: For the educators gathered in Pierrefonds, the decisions are not seen as final, but as liable to be revised at any moment. This uncertainty feeds a constant fear. “I don’t trust it,” says L.C. “I’m going back in, but I don’t trust it.”
Farida H., éducatrice à Laval, fait part: Farida H., an educator in Laval, is among those who could not benefit from the acquired rights clause. She says her administration contacted her to put an immediate choice before her: “‘What’s your decision? Are you coming back Monday without the religious symbol or not?’ I said: ‘No, I’m not taking off my scarf.’”
Depuis, aucune confirmation écrite. Cett: Since then, there has been no written confirmation. This lack of a clear status prevents her from pursuing any recourse. “Without the official dismissal, I can’t do much […] even to contact the union to file a grievance.”
Son cas met en lumière une autre zone d’: Her case highlights another area of confusion: that of employees who cannot claim the acquired rights clause because of their hiring date, even though they had already started their careers in the school system. Trained in early childhood education techniques, M<sup>s</sup>. Hocine worked in her field in Montréal before being recruited by the Laval CSS after a move. That change of employer put her in the category of “new hires,” without acquired rights. “I filed appeals […] I changed employers because I had to […] but they didn’t accept it.” She sums it up: “We don’t understand what’s going on […] it’s a double standard.”
À Montréal, Hajar Bouras décrit une situ: In Montréal, Hajar Bouras describes a different but equally opaque situation. After eight years in daycare, she was hired in September 2025 by the Centre de services scolaire de Montréal. She says that on the day of her job interview, she explicitly asked about wearing the veil. “I said: ‘I’m a veiled woman. Is that okay or not?’ […] They answered: ‘No, no, there’s no problem at all.’”
Quelques mois plus tard, après l’entrée: A few months later, after the measures came into effect, she was summoned by her administration and invited to sign a consent form to remove her religious symbol. She refused. “They gave me five days to think about it […] After that, I never got any answer.” Since then, her file is still active, but no formal decision has been made. “There’s no closing of the file, nothing.”
Comme dans le cas de Farida H., cette ab: As in Farida H.’s case, this lack of status blocks any action on Hajar Bouras’s part. But for her, there is also an earlier breach: a verbal commitment made at the time of hiring that was not honoured.
Au-delà de la situation administrative,: Beyond the administrative situation, she describes an immediate shock. “The first day, it was a shock for me. I cried, I couldn’t even stop.” And there are concrete consequences: no income, and an employment insurance claim still being processed.
Cette situation déborde en outre sur la: This situation also spills over into family life. Her daughter, who also wears the veil, is questioning her future in Quebec. “She said to me: ‘What are we even doing here? […] We’re going to change provinces, we’re going to leave the country!’”
<strong>Des enseignantes du CSSMB égalem: Teachers at the CSSMB also left in limbo
Des enseignantes relevant du Centre de s: Teachers from the Centre de services scolaire Marguerite-Bourgeoys (CSSMB) were also present at this meeting. Yet they are not covered by Bill 94. Their presence is explained by a very recent development: they say they received a letter with a form to fill out, which introduced ambiguity about their status.
Dans ce document, il est indiqué que « l: The document states that “since teaching staff have remained subject to the Act respecting the laicity of the State since its adoption in 2019, the individuals concerned must also fill out the form if they wish to have an acquired right recognized.” Further on, the letter specifies: “Only individuals who have received a favourable decision from the Human Resources Department will be considered as benefiting from an acquired right.”
Cette formulation, appliquée indistincte: This wording, applied indiscriminately to all staff, has sown doubt among some teachers who wear the hijab. While their legal status falls under a different framework, being invited to have an “acquired right” recognized in this context is perceived as a contradictory signal.
Contacté par La Converse, le CSSMB a con: Contacted by La Converse, the CSSMB confirmed by email that the letter was indeed sent on April 2 and that its aim was, among other things, to obtain an accurate picture of the situation, school by school. “This includes staff members who already have acquired rights, since these must be validated and documented under the new provisions,” it explains.
Une analyse individualisée est rendue né: An individualized analysis is necessary, it says, because in some cases an employee may hold several positions (teaching and supervision, or other duties). That said, the CSSMB tries to be reassuring, specifying that “receiving the form does not mean that a person’s acquired rights are being called into question, but rather that an administrative validation is required in the context of the evolving legal framework.”
L’application de la loi 94 dans sa premi: The application of Bill 94 in its first version had set off a wave of panic among parents whose children are in daycare. A Léger poll commissioned by the Association des garderies privées du Québec (AGPQ) and recently made public reveals that<l1> two-thirds of Quebec parents are comfortable with, or consider acceptable, an educator wearing a religious symbol in daycare</l1>.
Le gouvernement s’est-il trompé sur ce c: Did the government get this wrong? In any case, this accumulation of experiences feeds a broader disappointment. The system, at first seen as protective, now appears unstable. “They put us in a situation of uncertainty,” says L.C. “I’ve lost trust.”
Et l’incertitude ne se limite pas au pré: And the uncertainty is not limited to the present. It affects medium-term plans. Changing positions, accepting a promotion, taking a training course: every decision becomes risky, because it can mean losing acquired rights.
Certaines hésitent à poursuivre leur pro: Some hesitate to pursue professional advancement. Others are considering a complete career change. “We’ll do what we can, not what we want,” says L.C. For some, the reflection goes further. The idea of leaving Quebec emerges, mentioned in connection with loved ones who have already left or are about to. Families find themselves separated, and individual paths are redrawn under constraint.
